A.explanation: Pressure has units of $\text{Pa}$, not $\text{N}$, so $(p_b - p_t)$ alone cannot equal a force such as upthrust.

B.explanation: Upthrust is the net upward force from the water, equal to upward force $p_b A$ minus downward force $p_t A$.

C.explanation: Subtracting $W$ gives the resultant net force on the block, not the upthrust exerted by the water alone.

D.explanation: Adding $W$ mixes the weight of the wood with the fluid forces, whereas upthrust depends only on $p_b$, $p_t$ and $A$.

hints: Notice the block has the same cross-sectional area $A$ at the top where pressure is $p_t$ and at the bottom where pressure is $p_b$, with $p_b$ greater because it is deeper.
Recall that pressure is force per unit area, so the water pushes down on the top with force $p_t A$ and pushes up on the bottom with force $p_b A$.
Consider what you get when you subtract the downward fluid force from the upward fluid force, and keep the weight $W$ separate because it is due to gravity not the water.
walkthrough: Identify the two fluid forces on the flat ends: downward force on top is $F_t = p_t A$ and upward force on bottom is $F_b = p_b A$, both in $\text{N}$.
State the rule for upthrust: it is the resultant force exerted by the fluid, equal to upward thrust minus downward thrust because they act in opposite directions.
Set up the subtraction: $U = F_b - F_t = p_b A - p_t A$.
Factorise to $U = (p_b - p_t)A$ and check units: pressure in $\text{Pa}$ times area in $\text{m}^2$ gives force in $\text{N}$.
Note that $W$ is the weight of the wood acting downward and is not part of the fluid upthrust, so options that add or subtract $W$ describe net force, not upthrust.
